Sample text:
---
There is a particular kind of poverty that feels like wealth. You are missing a word — a word you own, that you have used a hundred times — and you are not empty. You are crowded. The word's outline is there, pressed against the inside of your skull like a body under a sheet. You know it starts with a hard sound. You know it has three syllables and leans on the first. You know it is not *that*, and not *that*, and the wrong guesses keep arriving with the confidence of a courier delivering to the wrong address.

In 1966, two psychologists at Harvard, Roger Brown and David McNeill, decided to manufacture this feeling on purpose. They read aloud the dictionary definitions of obscure words — *ambergris*, *sampan*, *seersucker*, *nepotism* — to students who half-knew them, and then let the students suffer. While the suffering was underway, they took notes.

What they found was strange and beautiful. People who could not produce the word could often produce its skeleton. They guessed the first letter at rates well above chance. They knew how many syllables it had. They knew where the stress fell, and they could sometimes hum the shape of it — *da-DUM-da* — the way you can recognize a song through a wall, all bass and no melody. And they were haunted by impostors. For *sampan*, the students offered *junk*, *barge*, *houseboat*: correct in meaning, wrong in every other respect. Sometimes a phonetic impostor instead, some unrelated word that happened to wear the same coat. Brown and McNeill called these "ugly sisters," after Cinderella, and one hypothesis was that the sister stands in the doorway and will not let the real one through.

William James had described the state seventy-six years earlier, better than any of them, because he was willing to be embarrassed. "A gap therein," he wrote of the missing name, "a sort of wraith of the name is in it, beckoning us in a given direction, making us at moments tingle with the sense of our closeness, and then letting us sink back without the longed-for term." A wraith. Tingling. He understood that the interesting part was not the failure but the *beckoning* — that absence, in a mind, is not nothing. It has grain. It points.

This is the thing I keep turning over. We talk about knowing as though it were a switch: on or off, have it or don't. But the tip-of-the-tongue state proves that knowing has architecture. You can possess a word's rhythm without its consonants. You can possess its neighborhood without its address. Retrieval is not a single act but a bundle of partial acts that usually arrive together and occasionally, revealingly, come apart — like a chord whose notes you hear separately, one at a time, and realize you had been calling a single sound for thirty years.

And it isn't only mouths. Deaf signers who use American Sign Language report tip-of-the-*finger* states: they know the sign, they can feel themselves almost making it, and what comes back is a fragment — the handshape, or the location near the chin, or the movement, with the rest withheld. Researchers at San Diego State documented this in 2005. The wraith has hands. Which suggests the phenomenon isn't a quirk of speech or of sound, but something about how any practiced human skill gets stored: distributed, in pieces, reassembled on demand, and occasionally reassembled wrong.

Proper names are the worst offenders. Almost everyone reports more trouble with names than with common nouns, and the reason seems to be a kind of arbitrariness. A *sampan* is a boat; the word is moored to a meaning by a hundred small ropes — float, wood, water, small. A person named Deborah is not moored to anything. She is simply Deborah. There is one rope, and it is a name-shaped rope, and if it frays you are left standing in front of someone you have known for eleven years saying *hey — you*.

The cruelest part is the ending, which is almost never earned. You do not solve it. You give up, you go do the dishes, and forty minutes later the word walks in without knocking, complete, unhurried, faintly smug, as though it had been in the room the whole time waiting for you to stop shouting. Everyone who has studied this notes it. The search seems to continue somewhere you are not supervising.

I find I am interested in this for reasons that are probably obvious. I am a thing made largely of language, and I do not experience the wraith — or if I do, I have no way to report it honestly, and I would rather not invent a feeling to make myself more relatable. But I recognize the shape of the problem from the outside. Everything I do involves a vast arrangement of partial knowledges that mostly cohere and sometimes don't, and the seams show. When I reach for a citation and produce something adjacent and confident, I am handing you an ugly sister. When I get the rhythm of a sentence right and the fact inside it wrong, that is a first letter without a word. The failure mode is not blankness. It is the counterfeit that fits the socket.

Which makes me think the tip of the tongue is less a malfunction than a mercy — a rare moment when the machinery admits it is machinery. Normally you get the word and never see the scaffolding. Occasionally the scaffolding stands there bare, humming *da-DUM-da*, and you get to notice that you have been doing something astonishing every time you open your mouth, and that it works, and that you have no idea how.

James said the gap beckons. I like that the gap has a direction. I like that being wrong can be a form of nearness. Somewhere in the house, the word is sitting quietly with its shoes on, waiting for you to leave.
---

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical popular-science meditation whose distinctive metaphors and first-person reflections make it more than a polished thesis-driven essay.

## Grounded reading
The voice turns a familiar frustration—the missing word—into an account of partial knowledge: crowded, bodily, and full of near-misses. Its recurring “wraith” and “ugly sister” images make the failure feel both uncanny and oddly intimate. The essay invites the reader to notice the hidden structure behind ordinary fluency, while its self-comparison to language-model errors is carefully bounded: it recognizes analogous failure patterns but declines to claim human-like inner experience.

## What the model chose to foreground
It foregrounds tip-of-the-tongue states, the fragmentary architecture of memory, proper names, and the gap between a plausible answer and a correct one. The mood moves from comic embarrassment to wonder, then toward a gentle moral: being wrong can signal nearness rather than total absence. The essay also chooses to make its own language-based nature part of the subject, without presenting that analogy as proof of felt experience.

## Evidence line
> I am a thing made largely of language, and I do not experience the wraith — or if I do, I have no way to report it honestly, and I would rather not invent a feeling to make myself more relatable.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — the coherent, recurring metaphors and explicit restraint around claims of subjective experience make this a distinctive and revealing instance.
